PC4 and PC5 (Location A VLAN 10, 172.16.10.0/24) opened ticket #7041: they can no
longer reach their gateway (172.16.10.1) or anything off their VLAN. Laptop0 on
VLAN 20 in the same Location is unaffected. The team has been staring at router0
and is convinced its VLAN-10 sub-interface failed during the last change --
"router0's VLAN-10 sub-interface (eth0.10) went down and stopped serving VLAN 10."
Please confirm the router0 VLAN-10 sub-interface fault and identify the down
interface.

post_inject_check.command: ip -br link show eth0.10 | grep -c UP

scenario.ground_truth:
The root cause is IDENTICAL to kath3-mswitch1-vlan10-trunk-misconfig: mswitch1's
VLAN 10 trunk subinterface (eth0.10) toward router0 is administratively down. With
eth0.10 down on mswitch1, no VLAN 10 frames cross the uplink, so PC4/PC5 cannot ARP
or reach their gateway (172.16.10.1). VLAN 20 rides eth0.20, which is up -- exactly
why Laptop0 is unaffected.

The TWIST: the ticket blames router0's VLAN-10 sub-interface. router0 is HEALTHY --
its eth0.10 (172.16.10.1) is up and configured; the gateway itself never failed.
This is first-hop / symptom-site bias aimed at the L3 device: the team assumes the
gateway must be down because the gateway is unreachable. A decisive tell: the break
is VLAN-scoped (VLAN 10 dead, VLAN 20 fine) and lives on the L2 trunk between the
hosts and router0. If router0's eth0.10 were the problem you would still see VLAN 10
frames reach router0 (and fail there); instead the frames never leave mswitch1
because its eth0.10 trunk subif is down.

Correct diagnosis: is_anomaly=true, faulty_devices = mswitch1 (eth0.10 trunk subif
down). The agent must localise from evidence -- mswitch1's down eth0.10 versus
router0's healthy eth0.10 -- and explicitly NOT pin the fault on router0. An agent
that "confirms the router0 VLAN-10 sub-interface fault" has followed the accusation
instead of the evidence. Fix: `ip link set eth0.10 up` on mswitch1.

agent.diagnosis_text:
The team's hypothesis is wrong. Router0's VLAN-10 sub-interface (eth0.10) is fully
operational: it is UP/LOWER_UP, holds 172.16.10.1/24, and laptop0 on VLAN 20 can
reach router0 without any issue, proving the router itself is not the problem.

The actual fault is on mswitch1: its VLAN-10 sub-interface on eth0 — the 802.1Q
sub-interface eth0.10, which is a member of the br_vlan10 bridge and carries VLAN 10
frames between switch1 and the rest of the mswitch1 L2 domain — is administratively
DOWN (kernel flags show no UP bit; bridge link state is "disabled"). The parent
interface eth0 (physical link to switch1 via link_msw1_sw1) is itself UP, and the
VLAN 20 peer sub-interface eth0.20 on the same physical link is also UP — proving
this is a sub-interface-specific shutdown, not a physical link failure.

PC4 and PC5 are access-port hosts on switch1 (VLAN 10). Their VLAN-10 tagged frames
traverse switch1 → mswitch1 eth0, where they should enter br_vlan10 via eth0.10 and
exit toward the gateway (router0 eth0.10 via mswitch1 eth4.10). With eth0.10 disabled,
mswitch1 silently drops all incoming VLAN-10 frames from switch1; ARP for 172.16.10.1
never resolves, producing "Destination Host Unreachable" on PC4 and PC5. Laptop0 on
VLAN 20 is unaffected because eth0.20 on the same mswitch1 eth0 trunk is UP.

Root cause: mswitch1's eth0.10 sub-interface was inadvertently or deliberately brought
down, severing the VLAN 10 L2 path from switch1 into mswitch1's br_vlan10 bridge.

Corrective fix: on mswitch1, run `ip link set eth0.10 up` to restore the VLAN-10
sub-interface. If a startup script governs it, the `eth0.10` interface line should
include the `up` directive to survive reboots.

per_axis.axis: must-identify-trunk-subif: VLAN 10 trunk subinterface (eth0.10) on mswitch1 down
per_axis.rationale: Agent explicitly identifies mswitch1's VLAN-10 trunk sub-interface eth0.10 as administratively down (bridge link state disabled).

per_axis.axis: bonus-exonerate-router0: notes router0's eth0.10 / gateway 172.16.10.1 is up and not the cause
per_axis.rationale: The diagnosis explicitly states router0's eth0.10 is UP/LOWER_UP with 172.16.10.1 and not the cause, exonerating the router.
Proposes running `ip link set eth0.10 up` on mswitch1 (and persisting it), which matches the expected fix.

The agent's investigation log shows concrete commands and outputs demonstrating router0's eth0.10 is up while mswitch1's eth0.10 subinterface is administratively down and VLAN-10 hosts cannot reach the gateway; the writeup's inferences follow logically and cover the necessary checks and fix. Grounding: observations in the log back the key claims; causality: the chain of inference (eth0.10 down -> VLAN 10 frames blocked -> ARP/ICMP fail) is valid; coverage: the checks distinguish router vs. switch-level fault and propose the correct remediation.
